description:
We are LEADERS, a team of engineering students passionate about space, AI, and innovation. For the Flame in Freefall challenge, we aim to turn NASA’s microgravity combustion data into an interactive AI-powered dashboard that reveals fire safety insights for future space missions.

Together, we turn complex data into insights for safer space exploration.
summary: Freefall turns decades of NASA microgravity fire experiments into hands-on simulations anyone can run in a browser. Twenty ISS combustion experiments, including FLEX, BASS, Saffire, SPICE and SAME, run on five shared physics engines: droplet, solid, burner, jet and smoke. Each engine is tuned to real results from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database and drives a 3D flame. Users change one thing at a time, such as oxygen, extinguisher gas or gravity, and see the effect, with real flight tests replayed beside the model’s prediction. A station view, the Freefall Fire Console, maps each result onto the ISS to show where it is a hazard or put to use. Every lab has a Result tab saying how far to trust the model; it matches burn outcomes in 84% of 261 FLEX tests. Fire behaves very differently in microgravity, and Freefall makes that knowledge clear for students, crews and future habitat designers.
details:
Freefall is an interactive lab for microgravity fire safety. A guided start explains each test, and one press of Ignite runs a simulated ISS burn. Beginner and Advanced modes let users go deeper; Advanced adds pressure, model-versus-measured comparisons and a map of every test. The Application tab and the Freefall Fire Console, a 3D ISS model, show where each result matters on the station.

How it works: Twenty NASA experiments share five physics engines. Droplet covers FLEX, FLEX-2 and CFI (261 FLEX tests, PSI-69; CFI constants, PSI-117). Solid covers BASS, BASS-II and Saffire I-III (Saffire-II samples, PSI-99). Burner covers s-Flame, Flame Design, CFI-G and BRE (PSI-10, PSI-159). Jet covers SPICE, SLICE, CLD Flame and E-FIELD Flames. Smoke covers SAME, SAME-R, DAFT and DAFT-2. A Python script turns NASA's tables into data files, and a custom shader renders the flame, matched frame by frame against NASA flight video.

Benefits and impact: Fire in microgravity spreads, smokes and goes out in ways that run against everyday intuition. Freefall makes decades of NASA research playable for students, future crews and Moon/Mars habitat designers, and links each result to real places and hazards on the station.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules, Three.js and Python. It runs as static files hosted on GitHub Pages, with no build step.

Creativity: Inspired by the play-first style of the University of Colorado's PhET simulations, Freefall adds real orbital measurements, side-by-side model vs. flight-data comparisons, and a 3D station view that connects each experiment to practice.

Factors we considered: Scientific honesty first. Burn endings match 219 of 261 FLEX tests (84%); silicone and Nomex are correctly predicted not to burn in orbit; burner flame temperatures average within 68 K of measurements. We state the limits too: the model does not predict ignition failures, and the Jet and Smoke labs show trends only. Every lab is labeled "illustrative." We also kept the interface simple, with two depth levels for different audiences.

Use of AI: The lab code was written with Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, under our team's direction and review. The optional in-app guide can use ChatGPT for wording only; every number comes from Freefall's own model.
